claim: The finding that systemic therapy for females with breast cancer may not add excess COVID-19 risk has important clinical implications while counselling and providing patient care during the pandemic.
source: Our finding suggests that systemic therapy for females with BC may not add excess COVID-19 risk. Multiple large cohort studies and meta-analysis of patients with cancer diagnosed with COVID-19 similarly did not identify active anti-cancer therapy, specifically chemotherapy, as a factor associated with adverse COVID-19 outcomes, which is consistent with our results (Garassino et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2020; Albiges et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2021; Jee et al., 2020). However, in contrast, some studies of patients with other cancers have shown a negative impact of chemotherapy (Grivas et al., 2021; Sharafeldin et al., 2021; Lièvre et al., 2020; Chavez-MacGregor et al., 2022) and immunotherapy use (Chavez-MacGregor et al., 2022). These findings have important clinical implications while counselling and providing patient care during the pandemic.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the clinical significance of the findings, supported by citations to consistent and contrasting literature.
